headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves after hours: FN, CLX, AAPL, PLTR Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Here are some of the companies making headlines in extended trading. Upwork – Shares of the freelance marketplace surged 10% on the back of a guidance raise. Full-year adjusted earnings are expected to range from $1.45 to $1.47 per share, topping the FactSet consensus of $1.39 per share. Palantir Technologies — Palantir shares were down 2% even after the company's third-quarter earnings topped Wall Street's estimates. Revenue for the period nearly doubled from a year earlier and surpassed $2 billion for the first time. The company's U.S. commercial revenue jumped 148% to $984 million, topping U.S. government revenue of $953 million. Palantir is also projecting about $2.65 billion in fourth-quarter revenue and $8.53 billion for full-year 2026. Lattice Semiconductor — The company's stock jumped 8% after Lattice solidly outpaced third-quarter revenue estimates and raised its forecast for the year. The semiconductor designer expects fourth-quarter revenue of between $325 million and $345 million, above the $293 million LSEG consensus estimate, and anticipates it will earn 82 cents to 86 cents per share after adjustments, topping the consensus estimate of 64 cents per share. The Clorox Company — The maker of Clorox Disinfecting Wipes added 2% after fiscal first-quarter results came in ahead of estimates. The company earned $1.55 per share on an adjusted basis on revenue of $1.91 billion. Analysts surveyed by LSEG were looking for $1.07 a share and $1.88 billion. Organic sales growth for the period also topped estimates. On Semiconductor — Shares fell about 2%. On Semiconductor said it would acquire Ferric, a maker of power converters, for $600 million in cash, plus up to $175 million in contingent consideration if certain revenue milestones are reached. Separately, the company said it expects fourth-quarter adjusted earnings in a range of 95 cents to $1.07 per share, while analysts polled by LSEG called for 95 cents per share. Apple — Apple shares were down around 3% in extended trading as revenue guidance for the December quarter disappointed traders. Apple sees revenue growth in a range of 7% to 10%, while analysts polled by LSEG anticipated 11.4% . Fabrinet – The provider of advanced optical packaging jumped more than 10% after current-quarter guidance trounced the Street's estimates. Fabrinet sees second-quarter adjusted earnings in a range of $4.77 to $4.92 per share on revenue of $1.6 billion to $1.65 billion. Analysts were looking for $4.43 a share and $1.48 billion, per FactSet. Ibotta — The digital consumer promotions company gained 13% after its fourth-quarter guidance beat analysts' expectations. Ibotta sees revenue in a range of $94 million to $98 million, beating the FactSet consensus estimate of $93.4 million. Adjusted EBITDA also topped expectations. CNBC's Deena Zaidi, Scott Schnipper, Christina Cheddar Berk and Nick Wells contributed reporting.

On the earnings call, Apple said it expects revenue to increase between 7% and 10% on an annual basis in the December quarter, compared to the 6.1% average analyst estimate, according to LSEG. The company's gross margin forecast for the current quarter is 45% to 46%, trailing the 46.3% average estimate. Revenue in the past quarter rose 12% from $102.5 billion a year earlier, Apple said in a statement on Monday. Apple's iPhone revenue in the quarter only included eight days of new Phone 18 Pro sales. And Apple's new flagship device, the iPhone Duo, didn't hit store shelves until the period was over. Monday's report includes a full quarter of higher-priced Apple products, as the company raised prices across the board in June after it signaled challenges with memory supply and other parts. Apple increased prices on iPhones by $100. The iPhone maker is reckoning with a global memory crunch and a rush for computer components. Apple said on Monday that its memory costs were higher this quarter than in the June period. Still, Ternus said in a statement that Apple had just capped off its "best fiscal year ever." Ternus told CNBC's MacKenzie Sigalos that Apple's growth came in spite of supply constraints and foreign exchange headwinds. "I think at this point, with everything we've achieved, it just feels like we've never been more confident that the best is yet to come," Ternus said. Ternus said that Apple "reluctantly" raised prices, which helped it offset component costs. Apple said tariff refunds added 5 cents to earnings per share. headlines.article_text: Palantir (PLTR) earnings Q3 2026 Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Palantir reported Q3 earnings that topped Wall Street's estimates. U.S. commercial revenue more than doubled and surpassed U.S. government revenue for the first time. The company has seen a boost from heightened demand for artificial intelligence tools. In this article PLTR Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 1:24 01:24 Palantir beats on earnings and revenue, Q3 commercial revenue surpasses government revenue Closing Bell: Overtime Palantir beat Wall Street's third-quarter estimates after the bell on Monday, with U.S. commercial revenue topping government for the first time as businesses adopt more of the company's artificial intelligence tools. Shares dipped about 3% in extended trading. Here's how the company did compared to LSEG estimates: Earnings per share : 44 cents adjusted vs. 41 cents expected Revenue : $2.31 billion vs. $2.18 billion expected Revenue nearly doubled from a year ago and blew past $2 billion for the first time ever, Palantir said. Net income more than doubled to $1.13 billion, or 44 cents per share, from about $476 million, or 18 cents per share. "I don't believe anyone's had consistent results like this in the history of software AI, ever," CEO Alex Karp told CNBC's Seema Mody in an interview, adding that the business is succeeding without salespeople. Palantir has long been known for its strength in the government sector, but its commercial segment caught up in Q3. U.S. commercial revenue jumped 148% to $984 million, surpassing U.S. government revenue of $953 million, which was up 96%. The company's U.S. commercial revenue has more than quintupled over the last two years. Palantir lifted its guidance, saying it now expects U.S. commercial revenue "in excess of" $3.56 billion for the full year. Last quarter, the company boosted its forecast to $3.42 billion. The company projects about $2.65 billion in revenue for the fourth quarter and about $8.53 billion for full-year 2026. Karp has openly supported the use of open-weight models and criticized leading AI labs, which he told CNBC earlier this year are forcing businesses to sell their data sovereignty. Karp, on Monday, also reiterated recent calls to nationalize AI labs, calling it the "only realistic way" to manage liability. In September, Karp joined major tech CEOs at the White House as calls for regulation mounted following claims from AI researchers that the technology has a more than 10% of killing humanity . "My message to everybody is: Beware of thinking you can delay the future in AI," he told CNBC. "The future is here. The political ramifications of it are here." Palantir stock chart. headlines.summary: Intel’s turnaround now hinges on proving its foundry strategy can deliver, as customers look for signs the company will add fab capacity and catch TSMC
headlines.article_text: Intel foundry faces critical test after stock's 45% plunge in October Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Intel's 29% drop on Friday left the stock down 45% in October, its worst month on record, according to FactSet. Intel sees the global market for server CPUs growing fivefold to $200 billion in the next five years, but the softening PC market is hurting legacy revenue. Intel is redirecting some 18A capacity in Oregon fabs to make Intel 3 chips for its server CPUs In this article INTC TSM Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Intel Corp. CEO Lip-Bu Tan attends the company's event in Tokyo, Japan, Oct. 7, 2026. Akio Kon | Bloomberg | Getty Images As Intel comes off its steepest stock drop since the 1970s due to a worsening outlook for the PC market, the chipmaker is facing intensifying pressure to get its flailing foundry business off the ground. It's been an elusive task for Intel. The company has spent half a decade, and a good chunk of its $108 billion in capital expenditures over that stretch, trying to challenge Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. But it still has no marquee customer for its most advanced chips and is primarily manufacturing chips for its own products. Wall Street is losing patience. After the U.S. government took a 10% stake in Intel in August 2025, and Nvidia followed with a $5 billion investment, the stock started to shoot up, ultimately rising sixfold over 10 months before peaking in June. Intel was finally finding its niche in the artificial intelligence boom, delivering central processors used for agentic AI, while optimism simultaneously grew over its fab aspirations. Intel's story took a dramatic turn for the worse on Thursday, when the company said revenue this quarter will be between $1 billion and $2 billion shy of analysts' estimates as the PC market continues to suffer from soaring costs for memory and other components. Intel still counts on its PC segment for roughly half of its revenue, and consumers are increasingly choosing not to upgrade. The stock plummeted 29% on Friday, its worst day since the 1970s, capping off a 45% plunge in October, the steepest monthly drop on record, according to FactSet. It's down another 8% in Monday trading. Intel vs. Nasdaq since start of October Intel's investments in the future are supposed to be paying off. CEO Lip-Bu Tan said he sees the global market for server processors increasing as much as five times over the next five years to about $200 billion. Intel's data center business recorded 78% growth in the third quarter from a year earlier to $7.3 billion. However, Intel said it can't make enough chips to fill demand, pointing to industrywide supply constraints for wafers, substrates and memory, many of the same factors hurting PC sales. That's forcing Tan to make some hard choices. In response to the capacity shortage, Intel said it's shifting some Oregon factory capacity away from making wafers for its advanced 18A chips to make more wafers on an older node, known as Intel 3, used for its data center products. Intel is counting on 18A to attract outside foundry customers, so the shift in resources could complicate that effort. David Yoffie, a Harvard Business School professor who previously spent almost three decades on Intel's board, said the latest moves are hardly welcoming to prospective foundry customers. "They're concerned that if Intel doesn't actually have excess capacity beyond its own demand, that they're just not a very credible supplier," Yoffie said. If it doesn't find a large-scale foundry customer within a year, "then the stress on Intel's economics are going to start to show even more dramatically," he said. Intel didn't respond to a request for comment. Intel is best known for its industry-leading central processing units, or CPUs. Graphics processing units from Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices ruled the early AI boom because they excel at handling large workloads for training models and inference for chatbots, while CPUs like Intel's are crucial for running the virtual machines used by agentic apps like Meta 's Muse. Competitor or partner? As one of the only companies in the world capable of manufacturing and packaging the advanced chips it needs for its own products, Intel has "more control over their destiny" than most chipmakers, Jordan Klein, an analyst at Mizuho Securities, said in an interview. "If you don't have enough capacity, you leave revenue and money on the table," Klein said. Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger, who was ousted in late 2024, spent his four-year tenure at the company aggressively pursuing foundry investments to catch up after delays on its 7- and 10-nanometer technologies, advanced process nodes that aim to fit more transistors on each chip. Tan has taken a more cautious approach, limiting spending until customer demand is locked in. He said on Thursday that "a couple customers" would be announced in the coming two quarters. watch now VIDEO 16:50 16:50 Can Intel’s New Arizona Chip Fab Bring It Back From The Brink? Tech Intel's 18A chips, for its own use, are in high-volume production out of Arizona, with a second fab in the works. A first structural truss was just installed at Intel's new Ohio facility, although the project is nearly five years behind schedule . Another roadblock to getting new customers, Yoffie said, is that chipmakers like Broadcom and Qualcomm may hesitate to manufacture chips at a company that's also a competitor on the product side. "The right solution is for Intel to spin off the foundry business," Yoffie said, calling it "not only the best solution, but maybe the only solution." Klein said AMD is likely the only major chipmaker that isn't interested in manufacturing at Intel because the two companies compete directly in the CPU market. He called it a "competitive, secrecy, privacy issue." AMD reports third-quarter results after the bell on Tuesday. Yoffie said the U.S. needs Intel to succeed. "Ultimately, TSMC can only create maybe 20-25% of their global capacity in the United States and that will still take several years," he said. "If we have no American foundry and we run into any number of geopolitical problems, supply chain problems like we had under Covid, that is going to be bad for the country and bad for the American semiconductor industry."
